topics.title: Linear equations in three or more unknowns

classification.difficultyReason: Checks supplied values by substitution, including negative numbers, fractions and decimals.

content.prompt: Determine whether:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=2+3\\\text{LHS}&=5\\\text{RHS}&=5\end{align*}$$Since LHS = RHS, $x=2$ is a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=4-(-2)\\\text{LHS}&=6\\\text{RHS}&=7\end{align*}$$Since LHS $\ne$ RHS, $x=-2$ is not a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=3(4-2)\\\text{LHS}&=6\\\text{RHS}&=6\end{align*}$$Since LHS = RHS, $x=4$ is a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=4\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)+3\\\text{LHS}&=6\\\text{RHS}&=5\end{align*}$$Since LHS $\ne$ RHS, $x=\frac{3}{4}$ is not a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=3+3\\\text{LHS}&=6\\\text{RHS}&=9-3\\\text{RHS}&=6\end{align*}$$Since LHS = RHS, $x=3$ is a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=2(-2)+8\\\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=-3(-2)-7\\\text{RHS}&=-1\end{align*}$$Since LHS $\ne$ RHS, $x=-2$ is not a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{3}{6}\\\text{LHS}&=\frac{1}{2}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{3+1}{9}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{4}{9}\end{align*}$$Since LHS $\ne$ RHS, $x=3$ is not a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=\frac{2}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{6}\\\text{LHS}&=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\\\text{LHS}&=2\\\text{RHS}&=2\end{align*}$$Since LHS = RHS, $x=2$ is a solution.
$$\begin{align*}\text{LHS}&=4(0.15)+0.2\\\text{LHS}&=0.8\\\text{RHS}&=2(0.15)+0.5\\\text{RHS}&=0.8\end{align*}$$Since LHS = RHS, $x=0.15$ is a solution.

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 1, Example 1 checks a proposed solution by substituting into LHS and RHS and comparing their values. Page 2 provides supporting equation context; cross multiplication on page 5 is not needed for these checks.
teachingContext.mappingNote: All parts directly assess verification by substitution: a checks addition; b negative substitution; c brackets; d a fractional value; e both sides; f a negative value on both sides; g fractional expressions on both sides; h a sum of fractions; i decimal expressions on both sides.

content.prompt: Solve each of the following equations by performing the same operation on each side:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x+3-3&=7-3\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x-5+5&=2+5\\x&=7\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x-9+9&=-5+9\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}3\times\frac{x}{3}&=3\times6\\x&=18\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}5\times\frac{x}{5}&=5\times(-6)\\x&=-30\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2x}{2}&=\frac{8}{2}\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{3x}{3}&=\frac{-7}{3}\\x&=-\frac{7}{3}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{-2x}{-2}&=\frac{3}{-2}\\x&=-\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Perform the same addition, subtraction, multiplication or division on both sides. Page 2 demonstrates explicit inverse operations and moving a negatively signed unknown to the other side before solving.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–d use addition or subtraction; e–h use multiplication or division; j divides by a negative coefficient. Parts i, k and l follow the page-2 method for a negatively signed unknown. The negative-coefficient skill is the most advanced directly assessed skill in this shared task.

All twelve results agree with the printed teacher answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies two or more inverse operations to equations containing fractions, negative coefficients, grouping and decimals.

content.prompt: Solve each of the following equations by performing two or more operations:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}2+4x&=3\\4x&=1\\x&=\frac{1}{4}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{3}+3-3&=4-3\\\frac{x}{3}&=1\\\frac{x}{3}\times3&=1\times3\\x&=3\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{3}-3+3&=-4+3\\\frac{x}{3}&=-1\\\frac{x}{3}\times3&=(-1)\times3\\x&=-3\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}8+2x&=12\\2x&=4\\x&=2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x+2}{3}\times3&=3\times3\\x+2&=9\\x+2-2&=9-2\\x&=7\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{4-x}{3}\times3&=2\times3\\4-x&=6\\6+x&=4\\x&=-2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{3-x}{5}\times5&=(-5)\times5\\3-x&=-25\\-25+x&=3\\x&=28\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides. Example 3 teaches successive inverse operations, multiplication to remove a denominator, and moving a negative unknown term to the other side to retain a positive coefficient. Example 5 supports dividing by an outer factor before expanding when convenient.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–c and e–f use successive inverse operations; d and i–l use the positive-coefficient rearrangement shown in Example 3(d); g–h add denominator removal and coefficient division; m–p remove the denominator before isolating x; q and s use the same operations with exact decimals; r and t divide by the outer decimal factor before undoing the inner operations. The most advanced assessed items require three inverse operations, so solve-linear-3-step is the closest primary catalogue skill.

content.prompt: Find the unknown number described in each of the following cases:

children.label: a
children.prompt: When an unknown number is added to 10, the result is 4.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}x+10&=4\\x+10-10&=4-10\\x&=-6\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: When 7 is subtracted from an unknown number, the result is $-3$.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}x-7&=-3\\x-7+7&=-3+7\\x&=4\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: When an unknown number is taken from 8, the result is $-3$.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}8-x&=-3\\x-3&=8\\x-3+3&=8+3\\x&=11\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: When twice an unknown number is added to 9, the result is 7.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}2x+9&=7\\2x+9-9&=7-9\\2x&=-2\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: When five is multiplied by the sum of an unknown number and 5, the result is 30.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}5(x+5)&=30\\x+5&=6\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: When 4 is taken from twice an unknown number, the result is $-11$.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}2x-4&=-11\\2x-4+4&=-11+4\\2x&=-7\\x&=-\frac{7}{2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: When twice an unknown number is taken from 3, the result is 6.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}3-2x&=6\\2x+6&=3\\2x&=-3\\x&=-\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: h
children.prompt: When the sum of an unknown number and 4 is divided by 3, the result is $-5$.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x+4}{3}&=-5\\x+4&=-15\\x&=-19\end{align*}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: When 3 is taken from half an unknown number, the result is 10.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{2}-3&=10\\\frac{x}{2}&=13\\x&=26\end{align*}$$

children.label: j
children.prompt: When 9 is added to one third of an unknown number, the result is 8.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the unknown number.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{3}+9&=8\\\frac{x}{3}&=-1\\x&=-3\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Represent the unknown by x and perform equivalent operations on both sides. For subtraction from a known number, move the unknown to obtain a positive coefficient. Undo grouped multiplication or division before isolating x where appropriate.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Every part requires constructing and solving an equation from words. Parts a–b use one inverse operation; c and g preserve reversed subtraction and collect the unknown positively; d and f use two operations; e undoes multiplication of a sum; h undoes division of a sum; i–j undo addition or subtraction before fractional scaling.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an average relationship into an equation with the unknown on both sides.

content.prompt: The average of two numbers is twice the smaller number. The larger number is 12. What is the smaller number?

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the smaller number.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{x+12}{2}&=2x\\x+12&=4x\\12&=3x\\x&=4\end{align*}$$

The smaller number is 4.

teachingContext.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides, clear the numerical denominator, then collect the unknown on one side, following Examples 3 and 4.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The average is the sum divided by two. Equating it to twice the smaller number creates a linear equation with the unknown on both sides.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows question 8 asking for the smaller number when the larger is 12 and the average is twice the smaller. The teacher image, under Chapter 2 Section A, prints '8. 4'. Independently solving (x+12)/2=2x gives x=4, agreeing with that entry.

classification.difficultyReason: Model two sums of consecutive integers with one unknown, equate them, then identify the middle integer.

content.prompt: A set of thirteen consecutive positive integers has the property that the smallest seven integers have the same sum as the largest six. What is the value of the middle integer?

inlines.text: Equate the two sums to find the smallest integer, then add 6.

answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the smallest integer. The smallest seven are $n,n+1,\ldots,n+6$, with sum $7n+21$. The largest six are $n+7,n+8,\ldots,n+12$, with sum $6n+57$.

$$\begin{align*}7n+21&=6n+57\\n+21&=57\\n&=36\end{align*}$$

The middle integer is the seventh integer:

$$\begin{align*}n+6&=36+6\\n+6&=42\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, collect the unknown on one side, and solve using the efficient algebraic steps demonstrated in Example 4.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The equal-sum condition produces a linear equation with the unknown on both sides; modelling the consecutive integers is the primary assessed skill.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student page shows question 9 about thirteen consecutive positive integers and equal sums of the smallest seven and largest six. The teacher image lists Section A question 9 as 42. Independently solving gives smallest integer 36 and middle integer 42, agreeing with the printed answer.

content.prompt: Solve each of the following equations for $x$:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x+a&=b\\x&=b-a\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x-a&=b\\x&=b+a\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{a}&=b\\x&=ab\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}ax&=b\\x&=\frac{b}{a}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&=c\\ax&=c-b\\x&=\frac{c-b}{a}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}ax-b&=c\\ax&=c+b\\x&=\frac{c+b}{a}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{a}+b&=c\\\frac{x}{a}&=c-b\\x&=a(c-b)\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{a}-b&=-c\\\frac{x}{a}&=b-c\\x&=a(b-c)\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}a-x&=b\\x+b&=a\\x&=a-b\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}a-bx&=c\\bx+c&=a\\bx&=a-c\\x&=\frac{a-c}{b}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x+a}{b}&=c\\x+a&=bc\\x&=bc-a\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{a-x}{b}&=c\\a-x&=bc\\x+bc&=a\\x&=a-bc\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}a(x+b)&=c\\x+b&=\frac{c}{a}\\x&=\frac{c}{a}-b\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{c}{a-b}$

Collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}ax&=bx+c\\ax-bx&=c\\(a-b)x&=c\\x&=\frac{c}{a-b}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{b}{a+c}$

Collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}ax&=b-cx\\ax+cx&=b\\(a+c)x&=b\\x&=\frac{b}{a+c}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{d-b}{a-c}$

Collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}ax+b&=cx+d\\ax-cx+b&=d\\ax-cx&=d-b\\(a-c)x&=d-b\\x&=\frac{d-b}{a-c}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{c+b}{a+d}$

Collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}ax-b&=c-dx\\ax+dx-b&=c\\ax+dx&=c+b\\(a+d)x&=c+b\\x&=\frac{c+b}{a+d}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{b-d}{a-c}$

Collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}ax-b&=cx-d\\ax-cx-b&=-d\\ax-cx&=b-d\\(a-c)x&=b-d\\x&=\frac{b-d}{a-c}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{cd-ab}{a-c}$

Expand, collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}a(x+b)&=c(x+d)\\ax+ab&=cx+cd\\ax-cx+ab&=cd\\ax-cx&=cd-ab\\(a-c)x&=cd-ab\\x&=\frac{cd-ab}{a-c}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\frac{ab-cd}{a+c}$

Expand, collect the $x$ terms and factor out $x$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}a(b-x)&=c(d+x)\\ab-ax&=cd+cx\\ax+cx+cd&=ab\\ax+cx&=ab-cd\\(a+c)x&=ab-cd\\x&=\frac{ab-cd}{a+c}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides, isolate the unknown, and expand brackets when appropriate. Examples 2–5 support the operation sequence; literal coefficients are retained exactly.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–m change the subject when it occurs once. Parts n–t gather repeated occurrences and factor out x, so change-subject-appears-twice is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill. As in the teacher answers, displayed quotient solutions assume their denominators are nonzero.

content.prompt: Solve for $x$ if:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=2-\frac{1}{3}\\x&=\frac{5}{3}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}2x&=\frac{1}{7}+3\\2x&=\frac{22}{7}\\x&=\frac{11}{7}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\\x&=\frac{8-3}{12}\\x&=\frac{5}{12}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}2x&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\\2x&=\frac{3}{4}\\x&=\frac{3}{8}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{2}&=2-\frac{1}{4}\\\frac{x}{2}&=\frac{7}{4}\\x&=\frac{7}{2}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{3}&=1+\frac{5}{6}\\\frac{x}{3}&=\frac{11}{6}\\x&=\frac{11}{2}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2x-x}{4}&=\frac{1}{3}\\\frac{x}{4}&=\frac{1}{3}\\x&=\frac{4}{3}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $12$.

$$\begin{align*}12x+6x+4x&=3\\22x&=3\\x&=\frac{3}{22}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{2}&=\frac{3}{8}-\frac{1}{4}\\\frac{x}{2}&=\frac{1}{8}\\x&=\frac{1}{4}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $6$.

$$\begin{align*}4x-1&=18\\4x&=19\\x&=\frac{19}{4}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $12$.

$$\begin{align*}9x+10&=1\\9x&=-9\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x&=2-3-\frac{1}{2}\\x&=-\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $4$.

$$\begin{align*}2(x+1)-1&=4\\2x+1&=4\\2x&=3\\x&=\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $2$.

$$\begin{align*}x-2+2x&=6\\3x&=8\\x&=\frac{8}{3}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $4$.

$$\begin{align*}2(x-1)-x&=8\\x-2&=8\\x&=10\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: When the digits of 14 are reversed to give 41, the result increases by 27.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find all two-digit numbers that increase by 27 when their digits are reversed.

answer.short:
14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69.

The units digit must be 3 greater than the tens digit.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be the tens digit and $B$ the units digit. The number is $10A+B$ and its reversal is $10B+A$.

$$\begin{align*}10B+A&=10A+B+27\\9B-9A&=27\\B-A&=3\\B&=A+3\end{align*}$$

Since $1\le A\le9$ and $0\le B\le9$, the possible tens digits are $1,2,3,4,5,6$. Hence the numbers are $14,25,36,47,58,69$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that there is no two-digit number that increases by 26 when its digits are reversed.

answer.short:
No such number exists.

Reversing the digits changes the number by a multiple of 9, and 26 is not divisible by 9.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be the tens digit and $B$ the units digit.

$$\begin{align*}10B+A&=10A+B+26\\9B-9A&=26\\9(B-A)&=26\end{align*}$$

Since $A$ and $B$ are whole numbers, $9(B-A)$ is divisible by 9. But 26 is not divisible by 9, so no such two-digit number exists.

content.prompt: Suppose $a>0$. Solve:

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&>c\\ax&>c-b\\x&>\frac{c-b}{a}\end{align*}$$
Since $a>0$, dividing by $a$ preserves the inequality direction.

$$\begin{align*}b-ax&\le c\\-ax&\le c-b\\x&\ge\frac{c-b}{-a}\\x&\ge\frac{b-c}{a}\end{align*}$$
Since $-a<0$, dividing by $-a$ reverses the inequality direction.

$$\begin{align*}a(x+b)&\ge c\\x+b&\ge\frac{c}{a}\\x&\ge\frac{c}{a}-b\end{align*}$$
Since $a>0$, dividing by $a$ preserves the inequality direction.

$$\begin{align*}a(b-x)&<c\\b-x&<\frac{c}{a}\\-x&<\frac{c}{a}-b\\x&>b-\frac{c}{a}\end{align*}$$
Dividing by positive $a$ preserves the direction; multiplying by $-1$ reverses it.

content.prompt: Let $x$ and $y$ be integers. Find the number of solutions $(x,y)$ to the inequality $x^2+y^2<5$.

inlines.text: 13 solutions.
Count the permitted integer values of
for each integer
from −2 to 2.

answer.worked:
Since $x^2$ and $y^2$ are non-negative, both $x^2<5$ and $y^2<5$. Thus $x,y\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$.

For $x=\pm2$, $y^2<1$, so $y=0$: 2 pairs.

For $x=\pm1$, $y^2<4$, so $y=-1,0,1$: 6 pairs.

For $x=0$, $y^2<5$, so $y=-2,-1,0,1,2$: 5 pairs.

$$2+6+5=13.$$

There are 13 solutions.

children.prompt: If two sides of a triangle have length 4, then what are the possible values for the length of the third side?

answer.short: $0<t<8$, where $t$ is the third side length.
answer.worked:
Let the third side have length $t$.

$$\begin{align*}t&<4+4\\t&<8\\4+t&>4\\t&>0\end{align*}$$

Therefore, $0<t<8$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many different (non-congruent) triangles have integer side lengths and a perimeter of 10 units?

answer.short:
2 triangles: side lengths $(2,4,4)$ and $(3,3,4)$ units.

The longest side must be less than half the perimeter.
answer.worked:
Write the integer side lengths as $a\le b\le c$.

$$\begin{align*}a+b+c&=10\\a+b&>c\\10-c&>c\\c&<5\end{align*}$$

Since $c$ is the longest side, $3c\ge10$. Hence $c=4$ and $a+b=6$. With $a\le b\le4$, the only pairs are $(a,b)=(2,4)$ and $(3,3)$. Both satisfy the triangle inequality.

There are 2 non-congruent triangles, with side lengths $(2,4,4)$ and $(3,3,4)$ units.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The integer side lengths of a triangle are $x+2$, $2x+7$ and $4x+1$. Find the greatest possible value of $x$.

answer.short:
$x=7$.

Apply all three triangle inequalities; the integer values satisfying them are $2\le x\le7$.
answer.worked:
Apply the triangle inequality to each side.

$$\begin{align*}(x+2)+(2x+7)&>4x+1\\3x+9&>4x+1\\x&<8\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}(x+2)+(4x+1)&>2x+7\\5x+3&>2x+7\\3x&>4\\x&>\frac43\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}(2x+7)+(4x+1)&>x+2\\6x+8&>x+2\\5x&>-6\\x&>-\frac65\end{align*}$$

Together, $\frac43<x<8$. Since $x+2$ is an integer, $x$ is an integer. The greatest possible value is $x=7$, giving positive side lengths $9$, $21$ and $29$, with $9+21>29$.

content.prompt: A rectangular room has a length that is 1 metre less than twice the width. If the perimeter of the room is 22 metres, then find its area.

answer.worked:
Let the width be $x$ metres. The length is $2x-1$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}2x+2(2x-1)&=22\\2x+4x-2&=22\\6x-2&=22\\6x&=24\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
The length is $2(4)-1=7$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}A&=lw\\A&=7\times4\\A&=28\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A sum of money is to be divided between three people. The first person receives one-fifth of the money, and the second person receives twice as much as the first person. This leaves $\$30$ for the third person. How much does each person receive?

answer.short: First person: $\$15$; second person: $\$30$; third person: $\$30$.
answer.worked:
Let the total be $x$ dollars. The first person receives $\frac{x}{5}$ dollars and the second receives $\frac{2x}{5}$ dollars.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{5}+\frac{2x}{5}+30&=x\\3x+150&=5x\\150&=2x\\x&=75\end{align*}$$
The first person receives $\$15$, the second receives $\$30$, and the third receives $\$30$.

content.prompt: One candle is 20 cm long and takes 4 hours to burn completely. A second candle is 30 cm long and takes 2 hours to burn completely. If both candles are lit at the same time, then find the time taken for the candles to have the same height.

answer.worked:
The burn rates are $20\div4=5$ cm/hour and $30\div2=15$ cm/hour. After $t$ hours, the heights are $20-5t$ cm and $30-15t$ cm.

$$\begin{align*}20-5t&=30-15t\\20+10t&=30\\10t&=10\\t&=1\end{align*}$$

The candles have the same height after 1 hour.

content.prompt: One candle is 12 cm long and takes 4 hours to burn completely. A second candle is 15 cm long and takes 3 hours to burn completely. If both candles are lit at the same time, then find the time taken for the first candle to be twice the height of the second candle.

answer.worked:
The burn rates are $12\div4=3$ cm/hour and $15\div3=5$ cm/hour. After $t$ hours, the heights are $12-3t$ cm and $15-5t$ cm.

$$\begin{align*}12-3t&=2(15-5t)\\12-3t&=30-10t\\12+7t&=30\\7t&=18\\t&=\frac{18}{7}\end{align*}$$

The first candle is twice the height of the second after $\dfrac{18}{7}$ hours.

content.prompt: One candle is 20 cm long and takes 3 hours to burn completely. A second candle is 25 cm long and takes 2 hours to burn completely. If both candles are lit at the same time, then find the time taken for the second candle to be exactly half the height of the first candle.

answer.worked:
The burn rates are $\dfrac{20}{3}$ cm/hour and $\dfrac{25}{2}$ cm/hour. After $t$ hours, the heights are $20-\dfrac{20}{3}t$ cm and $25-\dfrac{25}{2}t$ cm.

$$\begin{align*}25-\frac{25}{2}t&=\frac12\left(20-\frac{20}{3}t\right)\\150-75t&=60-20t\\150&=60+55t\\90&=55t\\t&=\frac{18}{11}\end{align*}$$

The second candle is half the height of the first after $\dfrac{18}{11}$ hours.

content.prompt: One candle is 15 cm long and takes 4 hours to burn completely. A second candle is 20 cm long and takes 3 hours to burn completely. If both candles are lit at the same time, find the time taken for the second candle to be exactly 1 cm shorter than the first candle.

answer.worked:
The burn rates are $\dfrac{15}{4}$ cm/hour and $\dfrac{20}{3}$ cm/hour. After $t$ hours, the heights are $15-\dfrac{15}{4}t$ cm and $20-\dfrac{20}{3}t$ cm. The second height must be 1 cm less than the first.

$$\begin{align*}20-\frac{20}{3}t&=15-\frac{15}{4}t-1\\240-80t&=168-45t\\240&=168+35t\\72&=35t\\t&=\frac{72}{35}\end{align*}$$

The second candle is 1 cm shorter than the first after $\dfrac{72}{35}$ hours.

inlines.text: Indian mathematicians working in the Middle Ages often composed their problems in lyrical passages. Solve the following problem, which appears in the 12th century text
Lilavati

O deer eyed one! Tell me, if one sixth of the number of bees in a colony entered a jasmine flower tree, one-third went to kadamba tree, one fourth flew to a mango tree, one-fifth went to a tree blooming with sampaka flowers, one-thirtieth went to a beautiful bed of lotuses bloomed by the sun’s rays and if the remaining one bee was roving about, how many total bees were there in the colony?

answer.short:
60 bees.

The five fractional shares total $\frac{59}{60}$, leaving $\frac{1}{60}$ of the colony as one bee.
answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the number of bees in the colony.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{n}{6}+\frac{n}{3}+\frac{n}{4}+\frac{n}{5}+\frac{n}{30}+1&=n\\10n+20n+15n+12n+2n+60&=60n\\59n+60&=60n\\60&=n\end{align*}$$
There are 60 bees in the colony.

teachingContext.mappingNote: The bee shares and remaining bee are modelled as quantities summing to the unknown colony size.

content.prompt: One jug has an unknown quantity of water. A second jug has 3 litres of water. One half of the contents of the first jug are transferred into the second jug, then one third of the contents of the second jug are transferred to the first jug. After which the two jugs contain the same amount of water. How much water was initially in the first jug?

answer.short:
3 litres.

Express each jug’s contents after both transfers and equate them.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ litres be the initial contents of the first jug. After the first transfer, the jugs contain $\frac{x}{2}$ and $3+\frac{x}{2}$ litres. After the second transfer, their contents are $\frac{x}{2}+\frac13(3+\frac{x}{2})$ and $\frac23(3+\frac{x}{2})$ litres.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{2}+\frac13\left(3+\frac{x}{2}\right)&=\frac23\left(3+\frac{x}{2}\right)\\3x+2\left(3+\frac{x}{2}\right)&=4\left(3+\frac{x}{2}\right)\\4x+6&=2x+12\\2x&=6\\x&=3\end{align*}$$
The first jug initially contained 3 litres.

teachingContext.mappingNote: The final jug contents are expressions in the initial first-jug volume; equality supplies the equation.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ litres be the initial contents of the first jug. After the first transfer, the jugs contain $\frac{3x}{4}$ and $4+\frac{x}{4}$ litres. After the second transfer, their contents are $\frac{3x}{4}+\frac14(4+\frac{x}{4})$ and $\frac34(4+\frac{x}{4})$ litres.

The first jug initially contained $\frac{16}{5}$ litres.

content.prompt: The rectangular paddock below is divided into eight identical rectangular paddocks. The total length of fencing used is 2100 metres. What is the total area?

spec.sourceRegion: Upper-left question 24, diagram beneath the stem.
spec.description: Landscape rectangle with eight identical rectangular regions: two upright rectangles on the upper left, three horizontal rectangles stacked centrally, one upright rectangle on the upper right, and two horizontal rectangles side by side along the bottom.
spec.mathematics: Each small rectangle has side ratio 1:3. The outer rectangle has proportional dimensions 6 by 4. Every outer and internal segment represents fencing, with shared segments counted once. Coordinate units establish proportions only and are not printed numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: No dimensions, labels or answers are shown.

inlines.text: Use the arrangement to find the side ratio, then count all fencing once.

answer.worked:
Let each small rectangle have width $x$ metres and length $y$ metres, with $y>x$. Comparing the total width along the top and bottom gives
$$\begin{align*}3x+y&=2y\\y&=3x.\end{align*}$$
Counting the outer boundary and each internal fence once gives a total fencing length of $6x+12y$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}6x+12y&=2100\\6x+12(3x)&=2100\\42x&=2100\\x&=50\\y&=3(50)\\y&=150.\end{align*}$$
The eight identical rectangles have total area
$$\begin{align*}A&=8xy\\A&=8(50)(150)\\A&=60\,000\text{ m}^2.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: The letters
through to
represent each of the numbers 0 through to 7 in some order. Find their values if:
Use the linked equations and the requirement that all eight values are distinct.

answer.worked:
From $A+C=A$, $C=0$. Since the values are distinct, $F\ne0$, so $FD=F$ gives $D=1$.

$$\begin{align*}B-G&=G\\B&=2G\end{align*}$$

Since $B\le7$ and neither $G=0$ nor $G=1$ is available, $G$ is 2 or 3. Also, $B\div H=G$ gives $H=2$. Hence $G\ne2$, because $G$ and $H$ have distinct values. Therefore $G=3$ and $B=6$.

The remaining values for $A$, $E$ and $F$ are 4, 5 and 7. From $A+H=E$ and $E-G=F$,

$$\begin{align*}E&=A+2\\F&=E-3\end{align*}$$

The only remaining pair differing by 2 is $A=5$, $E=7$. Thus $F=7-3=4$.

Therefore, $A=5$, $B=6$, $C=0$, $D=1$, $E=7$, $F=4$, $G=3$ and $H=2$.

content.prompt:
A system of equations may have more than one solution. Consider the following system of equations
$$\begin{aligned}2y-3x&=1\\3x-2y&=-1.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $(x,y)=(3,5)$ and $(x,y)=(1,2)$ are both solutions of this system of equations.

answer.worked:
For $(x,y)=(3,5)$:
$$\begin{align*}2y-3x&=2(5)-3(3)\\2y-3x&=1\\3x-2y&=3(3)-2(5)\\3x-2y&=-1.\end{align*}$$
For $(x,y)=(1,2)$:
$$\begin{align*}2y-3x&=2(2)-3(1)\\2y-3x&=1\\3x-2y&=3(1)-2(2)\\3x-2y&=-1.\end{align*}$$
Both pairs satisfy both equations, so both are solutions.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that for any real $t$, $(x,y)=\left(t,\frac12+\frac32t\right)$ is a solution of this system of equations.

answer.short: Substitution gives $2y-3x=1$ and $3x-2y=-1$ for every real $t$.
answer.worked:
Substitute $x=t$ and $y=\frac12+\frac32t$:
$$\begin{align*}2y-3x&=2\left(\frac12+\frac32t\right)-3t\\2y-3x&=1+3t-3t\\2y-3x&=1\\3x-2y&=3t-2\left(\frac12+\frac32t\right)\\3x-2y&=3t-1-3t\\3x-2y&=-1.\end{align*}$$
Both equations hold for every real $t$, so the given pair is a solution.

content.prompt: Solve each of the following for $(x,y)$ by equating each pair of equations.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(1,a+b)$, where $a\ne b$.

Equate the expressions for $y$, then substitute.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&=bx+a\\ax-bx&=a-b\\(a-b)x&=a-b\\x&=1\quad(a\ne b)\\y&=a(1)+b=a+b\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(1,a+b)$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(-\frac{b}{a},0\right)$, where $a\ne0$.

Equate the expressions for $y$, then substitute.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&=-ax-b\\2ax&=-2b\\x&=-\frac{b}{a}\quad(a\ne0)\\y&=a\left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)+b=0\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(-\frac{b}{a},0\right)$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(1,a-b)$, where $a\ne-b$.

Equate the expressions for $y$, then substitute.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}ax-b&=-bx+a\\ax+bx&=a+b\\(a+b)x&=a+b\\x&=1\quad(a\ne-b)\\y&=a(1)-b=a-b\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(1,a-b)$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(-ab,0)$, where $a\ne0$.

Equate the expressions for $y$, then substitute.
answer.worked:
The equations require $a\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{a}+b&=-\frac{x}{a}-b\\\frac{2x}{a}&=-2b\\x&=-ab\\y&=\frac{-ab}{a}+b=0\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(-ab,0)$.

content.prompt: Solve each of the following for $(x,y)$ using the substitution method.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(0,\frac{c}{b}\right)$, where $b\ne0$.

Substitute $x=by-c$ into the first equation. If $b=0$, there are no solutions unless $c=0$; then $(0,t)$ is a solution for every real $t$.
answer.worked:
Substitute $x=by-c$ into $x+by=c$.
$$\begin{align*}(by-c)+by&=c\\2by-c&=c\\2by&=2c\\y&=\frac{c}{b}\\x&=b\left(\frac{c}{b}\right)-c\\x&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y)=\left(0,\frac{c}{b}\right)$ for $b\ne0$.

If $b=0$, the equations require both $x=c$ and $x=-c$. There is no solution when $c\ne0$. When $c=0$, $x=0$ and $y$ is unrestricted.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(0,-\frac{c}{a}\right)$, where $a\ne0$.

Substitute $x=ay+c$ into the first equation. If $a=0$, there are no solutions unless $c=0$; then $(0,t)$ is a solution for every real $t$.
answer.worked:
Substitute $x=ay+c$ into $x+ay=-c$.
$$\begin{align*}(ay+c)+ay&=-c\\2ay+c&=-c\\2ay&=-2c\\y&=-\frac{c}{a}\\x&=a\left(-\frac{c}{a}\right)+c\\x&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y)=\left(0,-\frac{c}{a}\right)$ for $a\ne0$.

If $a=0$, the equations require both $x=-c$ and $x=c$. There is no solution when $c\ne0$. When $c=0$, $x=0$ and $y$ is unrestricted.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(1,a+b)$, where $a\ne b$.

Substitute $y=bx+a$ into the first equation. If $a=b$, every pair $(t,at+a)$ is a solution.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=bx+a$ into $y-ax=b$.
$$\begin{align*}(bx+a)-ax&=b\\(b-a)x+a&=b\\(b-a)x&=b-a\\x&=1\\y&=b(1)+a\\y&=a+b\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y)=(1,a+b)$ for $a\ne b$.

If $a=b$, both equations describe $y=ax+a$, so there are infinitely many solutions $(t,at+a)$, where $t$ is real.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(-1,a-b)$, where $a\ne-b$.

Substitute $y=bx+a$ into the first equation. If $a=-b$, every pair $(t,bt+a)$ is a solution.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=bx+a$ into $y+ax=-b$.
$$\begin{align*}(bx+a)+ax&=-b\\(a+b)x+a&=-b\\(a+b)x&=-(a+b)\\x&=-1\\y&=b(-1)+a\\y&=a-b\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y)=(-1,a-b)$ for $a\ne-b$.

If $a=-b$, both equations describe $y=bx+a$, so there are infinitely many solutions $(t,bt+a)$, where $t$ is real.

content.prompt: A coffee cart sells a total of 60 coffees for a total of $\$250$. Each regular coffee costs $\$3.50$ and each large coffee costs $\$5.50$. How many regular and how many large coffees are sold?

answer.worked:
Let $r$ be the number of regular coffees and $l$ the number of large coffees.
$$\begin{align*}r+l&=60 &&(1)\\3.5r+5.5l&=250 &&(2)\\3.5r+3.5l&=210 &&3.5\times(1)\\2l&=40 &&(2)-3.5\times(1)\\l&=20\\r&=60-20\\r&=40\end{align*}$$
Therefore, 40 regular coffees and 20 large coffees are sold.

Let $p$ be the number of pigs and $c$ the number of chickens.

There are 12 pigs and 11 chickens. Check: $12+11=23$ heads and $4(12)+2(11)=70$ legs.

content.prompt: A box contains twenty critters, and each is either a spider or a fly. If they have 138 legs in total, then how many spiders and how many flies are in the box?

answer.worked:
Let $s$ be the number of spiders and $f$ the number of flies. Spiders have eight legs and flies have six legs.

$$\begin{align*}s+f&=20 &&(1)\\8s+6f&=138 &&(2)\\6s+6f&=120 &&6\times(1)\\2s&=18 &&(2)-6\times(1)\\s&=9\\9+f&=20\\f&=11\end{align*}$$

There are 9 spiders and 11 flies. Check: $9+11=20$ and $8(9)+6(11)=138$.

content.prompt: In one day an elephant eats what a rabbit does in one year, taken to be 365 days. Together, in one day, they eat 100 kg of food. How many kilograms of food does the rabbit eat in one day?

answer.worked:
Let $r$ and $e$ be the amounts of food, in kilograms, eaten in one day by the rabbit and elephant respectively.
$$\begin{align*}e&=365r\\e+r&=100\end{align*}$$
Substitute $e=365r$ into the total-food equation.
$$\begin{align*}365r+r&=100\\366r&=100\\r&=\frac{100}{366}\\r&=\frac{50}{183}\end{align*}$$
The rabbit eats $\dfrac{50}{183}\text{ kg}$ of food in one day.

content.prompt: Solve these simultaneous equations for $(x,y)$ using the elimination method.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.

Therefore, $(x,y)=(1,-2)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}4y&=8\\y&=2\\x+2(2)&=3\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

Therefore, $(x,y)=(-1,3)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}6y&=12\\y&=2\\2x+2&=7\\2x&=5\\x&=\frac52\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\frac52,2\right)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.
$$\begin{align*}6x&=-3\\x&=-\frac12\\2\left(-\frac12\right)-3y&=-4\\-1-3y&=-4\\-3y&=-3\\y&=1\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(-\frac12,1\right)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}-2y&=8\\y&=-4\\x-4&=3\\x&=7\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(7,-4)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.
$$\begin{align*}-x&=5\\x&=-5\\2(-5)+y&=2\\y&=12\end{align*}$$

Add the equations to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}-7y&=14\\y&=-2\\4x-4(-2)&=11\\4x&=3\\x&=\frac34\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\frac34,-2\right)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.
$$\begin{align*}-2x&=4\\x&=-2\\5(-2)+2y&=-1\\2y&=9\\y&=\frac92\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(-2,\frac92\right)$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(-\frac{32}{21},-\frac17\right)$

Add the equations to eliminate $x$, then substitute for $y$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(-\frac13,-\frac89\right)$

Add the equations to eliminate $y$, then substitute for $x$.
answer.worked:
Add the equations to eliminate $y$.
$$\begin{align*}-6x&=2\\x&=-\frac13\\-\left(-\frac13\right)-3y&=3\\\frac13-3y&=3\\-3y&=\frac83\\y&=-\frac89\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(-\frac13,-\frac89\right)$.

$$\begin{align*}-2y&=-8\\y&=4\\2x-5(4)&=-7\\2x&=13\\x&=\frac{13}{2}\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\frac{13}{2},4\right)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.

Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$.

Add the equations to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=4\\\frac{x}{2}-4&=1\\\frac{x}{2}&=5\\x&=10\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(10,4)$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(20,-21)$

Add the equations to eliminate $y$, then substitute for $x$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{4}&=5\\x&=20\\\frac{20}{2}+\frac{y}{3}&=3\\10+\frac{y}{3}&=3\\\frac{y}{3}&=-7\\y&=-21\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$(x,y)=\left(\dfrac{c+d}{2a},\dfrac{c-d}{2b}\right)$, where $a,b\ne0$.

Add the equations to find $x$; subtract them to find $y$.
answer.worked:
Add the equations to eliminate $y$; subtract the second from the first to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}2ax&=c+d\\x&=\frac{c+d}{2a}\\2by&=c-d\\y&=\frac{c-d}{2b}\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\dfrac{c+d}{2a},\dfrac{c-d}{2b}\right)$, where $a,b\ne0$.

answer.short: No solution if $c\ne d$. If $c=d$, every pair satisfying $ax-by=c$ is a solution.
answer.worked:
Subtract the second equation from the first.
$$\begin{align*}(ax-by)-(ax-by)&=c-d\\0&=c-d\end{align*}$$
If $c\ne d$, the equations are inconsistent and have no solution. If $c=d$, the equations coincide: every pair satisfying $ax-by=c$ is a solution. For $a,b\ne0$, there are infinitely many such pairs.

Subtract the second equation from the first, then substitute $y=1$ into the second equation.
$$\begin{align*}by&=b\\y&=1\\ax+2b(1)&=2b\\ax&=0\\x&=0\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=(0,1)$, where $a,b\ne0$.

Add the equations to eliminate $y$; subtract the second from the first to eliminate $x$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2x}{a}&=3\\x&=\frac{3a}{2}\\\frac{2y}{b}&=1\\y&=\frac{b}{2}\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $(x,y)=\left(\dfrac{3a}{2},\dfrac{b}{2}\right)$, where $a,b\ne0$.

answer.worked:
Each game involves two teams, so the number of games is
$$\frac{12\times11}{2}=66.$$
Let $d$ be the number of draws. Each draw awards 2 points in total; each of the remaining $66-d$ games awards 3 points.
$$\begin{align*}2d+3(66-d)&=180\\2d+198-3d&=180\\198-d&=180\\d&=18\end{align*}$$
Therefore, 18 games finished in a draw.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(n-n^2,n^2+n)$; both values are integers.

Clear the denominators, eliminate one variable and substitute.
answer.worked:
Since $n\ne-1,0,1$, clear the denominators:
$$\begin{align*}nx+(n-1)y&=n(n-1)\qquad(1)\\(n+1)x+ny&=n(n+1)\qquad(2).\end{align*}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{align*}((n+1)x+ny)-(nx+(n-1)y)&=n(n+1)-n(n-1)\\x+y&=2n\\y&=2n-x.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{align*}nx+(n-1)(2n-x)&=n(n-1)\\x+2n(n-1)&=n(n-1)\\x&=-n(n-1)\\x&=n-n^2.\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}y&=2n-(n-n^2)\\y&=n^2+n.\end{align*}$$
Both $n-n^2$ and $n^2+n$ are integers whenever $n$ is an integer. Thus the system always has integer solutions for the permitted values of $n$.

$$\begin{align*}4z&=0\\z&=0\end{align*}$$
Subtract (1) from (3):
$$\begin{align*}2y+z&=0\\2y&=0\\y&=0\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{align*}x-0+0&=1\\x&=1\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y,z)=(1,0,0)$.

Number the equations (1), (2) and (3) in order. Subtract (2) from (3):
$$\begin{align*}x&=2\end{align*}$$
Subtract twice (1) from (2):
$$\begin{align*}-y&=5\\y&=-5\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{align*}2-5+z&=-4\\z-3&=-4\\z&=-1\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y,z)=(2,-5,-1)$.

Number the equations (1), (2) and (3) in order. Subtract (2) from (3):
$$\begin{align*}3y&=3\\y&=1\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (1) and (2):
$$\begin{align*}-2x+3+2z&=1\\-2x+2z&=-2\qquad(4)\\x+1+2z&=8\\x+2z&=7\qquad(5)\end{align*}$$
Subtract (4) from (5):
$$\begin{align*}3x&=9\\x&=3\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (5):
$$\begin{align*}3+2z&=7\\2z&=4\\z&=2\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y,z)=(3,1,2)$.

inlines.text: The following is known about the prices of peaches, pears and plums:
1 kg of peaches, 2 kg of pears and 3 kg of plums cost $26
1 kg of peaches, 1 kg of pears and 2 kg of plums cost $17
1 kg of peaches, 4 kg of pears and 1 kg of plums cost $24
Find the cost per kilogram of peaches, pears and plums, respectively.

answer.short: Peaches: $\$3$ per kg; pears: $\$4$ per kg; plums: $\$5$ per kg.
answer.worked:
Let $p$, $q$ and $r$ be the prices per kilogram of peaches, pears and plums, respectively, in dollars.
$$\begin{align*}p+2q+3r&=26\qquad(1)\\p+q+2r&=17\qquad(2)\\p+4q+r&=24\qquad(3)\end{align*}$$
Subtract (2) from (1) and from (3):
$$\begin{align*}q+r&=9\qquad(4)\\3q-r&=7\qquad(5)\end{align*}$$
Add (4) and (5):
$$\begin{align*}4q&=16\\q&=4\end{align*}$$
Substitute $q=4$ into (4):
$$\begin{align*}4+r&=9\\r&=5\end{align*}$$
Substitute $q=4$ and $r=5$ into (2):
$$\begin{align*}p+4+2(5)&=17\\p+14&=17\\p&=3\end{align*}$$
Peaches cost $\$3$ per kg, pears cost $\$4$ per kg and plums cost $\$5$ per kg.

Subtracting the second equation from the other two eliminates that price; adding the resulting equations eliminates the plum price. This models and solves a three-variable simultaneous word problem.

Substitution gives 3+8+15=26, 3+4+10=17 and 3+16+5=24.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate duck totals, leg contributions and the group relationship into three conditions, then combine them to isolate the lame-duck count.

content.prompt: A normal duck has two legs. A lame duck has one leg. A sitting duck has no legs. There are 33 ducks with 32 legs. The total number of normal ducks and lame ducks is twice the number of sitting ducks. How many lame ducks are there?

answer.worked:
Let $n$, $l$ and $s$ be the numbers of normal, lame and sitting ducks, respectively.
$$\begin{align*}n+l+s&=33 &&(1)\\2n+l&=32 &&(2)\\n+l&=2s &&(3)\end{align*}$$
Substitute (3) into (1):
$$\begin{align*}2s+s&=33\\3s&=33\\s&=11\\n+l&=22\end{align*}$$
Subtract $n+l=22$ from (2), then substitute:
$$\begin{align*}n&=10\\10+l&=22\\l&=12\end{align*}$$
There are 12 lame ducks.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate three pairwise sums into simultaneous equations and combine them using the taught method.

content.prompt: When three numbers are added in pairs, the results are 7, 11 and 2. Find the three numbers.

answer.worked:
Let the three numbers be $x$, $y$ and $z$.
$$\begin{align*}x+y&=7 &&(1)\\x+z&=11 &&(2)\\y+z&=2 &&(3)\\2x+2y+2z&=20 &&(1)+(2)+(3)\\x+y+z&=10 &&(4)\end{align*}$$
Subtract each pairwise sum from (4):
$$\begin{align*}x&=10-2\\x&=8\\y&=10-11\\y&=-1\\z&=10-7\\z&=3\end{align*}$$
The three numbers are $-1$, $3$ and $8$.

content.prompt: Find the values of $x$, $y$ and $z$ in the figure below if each of the unknowns is equal to the sum of its neighbours.

spec.description: Five unshaded circles in a horizontal chain, joined by short straight connectors at adjacent boundaries. Decorative cyan outlines and grey connectors are rendered in house black.
spec.mathematics: Labels from left to right are 1, x, y, z, 10. Adjacency gives x=1+y, y=x+z and z=y+10.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied endpoint values and unknown labels appear.

answer.short:
$(x,y,z)=(-10,-11,-1)$.

Express $x$ and $z$ in terms of $y$, then substitute into $y=x+z$.
answer.worked:
From the neighbouring circles,
$$\begin{align*}
x&=1+y\\
y&=x+z\\
z&=y+10.
\end{align*}$$
Substitute the expressions for $x$ and $z$ into the middle equation:
$$\begin{align*}
y&=(1+y)+(y+10)\\
y&=2y+11\\
-y&=11\\
y&=-11.
\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}
x&=1+(-11)\\
x&=-10\\
z&=-11+10\\
z&=-1.
\end{align*}$$
Thus $(x,y,z)=(-10,-11,-1)$.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that adding the purchase equations produces four copies of the requested combined price, using the taught sum method and the supplied warning about individual prices.

content.prompt: Ahmed walks into a shop and buys 1 kg of apples, 2 kg of bananas and 3 kg of carrots, spending $\$16$. Ben walks into the same shop and buys 3 kg of apples, 2 kg of bananas and 1 kg carrots, spending $\$20$. Connor walks into the same shop and buys 1 kg of apples, 1 kg of bananas and 1 kg of carrots. How much does she spend? Note: there is not enough information here to determine the individual prices.

answer.short:
$\$9$.

Add the two purchase equations and divide by 4.
answer.worked:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the prices per kilogram of apples, bananas and carrots, respectively, in dollars.

$$\begin{align*}a+2b+3c&=16\qquad\text{(1)}\\3a+2b+c&=20\qquad\text{(2)}\end{align*}$$

Adding (1) and (2):

$$\begin{align*}4a+4b+4c&=36\\a+b+c&=9\end{align*}$$

Connor spends $\$9$. The total can be found without determining the individual prices.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate three averages into simultaneous equations and eliminate variables to recover the ordered numbers.

content.prompt: The average of three numbers is 14. When the smallest of these is removed, the average of the two numbers that remain is 18. When the largest of these numbers is removed, the average of the two numbers that remain is 9. What are the numbers?

answer.worked:
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers in increasing order. The averages give
$$\begin{align*}x+y+z&=42 &&(1)\\y+z&=36 &&(2)\\x+y&=18 &&(3)\end{align*}$$
Subtract (2) from (1), then substitute into (3) and (2):
$$\begin{align*}x&=42-36\\x&=6\\6+y&=18\\y&=12\\12+z&=36\\z&=24\end{align*}$$
The numbers are $6,12,24$.

content.prompt: Anh and Bindi have $\$24$ between them. Anh gives Bindi $\$2$, and they now have the same amount of money. How much money did they each originally have?

answer.worked:
Let Anh originally have $x$ dollars and Bindi $y$ dollars.

$$\begin{align*}x+y&=24 &&(1)\\x-2&=y+2\\x-y&=4 &&(2)\\2x&=28 &&(1)+(2)\\x&=14\\14+y&=24\\y&=10\end{align*}$$

Anh originally had $\$14$ and Bindi $\$10$. After the transfer, each has $\$12$.

content.prompt: Sarah and Trang have $\$36$ between them. Sarah gives Trang $\$2$, but then still has twice as much as Trang. How much money did they each originally have?

answer.worked:
Let Sarah originally have $x$ dollars and Trang $y$ dollars.

$$\begin{align*}x+y&=36\\x-2&=2(y+2)\\x&=36-y\\36-y-2&=2(y+2)\\34-y&=2y+4\\30&=3y\\y&=10\\x&=36-10\\x&=26\end{align*}$$

Sarah originally had $\$26$ and Trang had $\$10$. After the transfer, they have $\$24$ and $\$12$, respectively, and $24=2\times12$.

content.prompt: If Casey were to give David $\$3$, then they would have the same amount of money. On the other hand, if Casey were to give David $\$12$, then David would have three times as much money as Casey. How much money do they each have?

answer.short:
Casey has $\$21$ and David has $\$15$.

Model both transfers with simultaneous equations and solve by substitution.
answer.worked:
Let Casey have $x$ dollars and David have $y$ dollars originally.

$$\begin{align*}x-3&=y+3\\x&=y+6\\y+12&=3(x-12)\\y+12&=3(y+6-12)\\y+12&=3y-18\\30&=2y\\y&=15\\x&=15+6\\x&=21\end{align*}$$

Therefore, Casey has $\$21$ and David has $\$15$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Define the original amounts, form equations from the transfers, substitute one unknown expressed in terms of the other, and solve using equivalent equations.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The two transfer conditions assess modelling and solving simultaneous equations, matching the substitution demonstration on page 17 and the money-transfer model visible on page 26.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows Casey giving David 3 dollars for equal amounts, or 12 dollars for David to have three times Casey's amount. The teacher image's Section F answer 3 states Casey has 21 dollars and David has 15 dollars. Independently derived values satisfy both conditions: 21−3=15+3=18, and 15+12=27=3(21−12).

classification.difficultyReason: Keep two alternative transfers and their opposite directions distinct, then impose equality in one case and a doubling relationship in the other.

content.prompt: If Annie gave Jacob $\$20$, then they would have the same amount of money. If Jacob gave Annie $\$22$, however, then Annie would then have twice as much as Jacob. How much money do they each have?

answer.short:
Annie has $\$146$ and Jacob has $\$106$.

Model both transfers with simultaneous equations and solve by substitution.
answer.worked:
Let Annie have $x$ dollars and Jacob have $y$ dollars.

$$\begin{align*}x-20&=y+20\\x&=y+40\\x+22&=2(y-22)\\y+40+22&=2(y-22)\\y+62&=2y-44\\y&=106\\x&=106+40\\x&=146\end{align*}$$

Annie has $\$146$ and Jacob has $\$106$. After the first transfer, each has $\$126$. After the second transfer, Annie has $\$168$ and Jacob has $\$84$, so Annie has twice as much.

classification.difficultyReason: Express both future ages in terms of the boy's current age, then solve a linear equation.

content.prompt: A boy is twenty years younger than his father. In five years time the father will be three times the age of the boy. How old is the boy currently?

answer.worked:
Let the boy's current age be $x$ years. His father's current age is $x+20$ years. In five years, their ages will be $x+5$ and $x+25$ years.

$$\begin{align*}x+25&=3(x+5)\\x+25&=3x+15\\25&=2x+15\\10&=2x\\x&=5\end{align*}$$

The boy is currently 5 years old. In five years, he will be 10 and his father will be 30, which is three times his age.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate original and hypothetical voter ratios into equations with different reductions, solve for both original counts and sum them.

content.prompt: The ratio of male to female voters in an election was $4:3$. Had 8 fewer men and 14 fewer women voted, the ratio would have been $2:1$. Find the total number of votes cast.

answer.short:
70 votes.

Form equations from the two ratios and solve by substitution.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ and $y$ be the original numbers of male and female voters respectively.

$$\begin{align*}3x&=4y &&(1)\\x-8&=2(y-14) &&(2)\\x-8&=2y-28\\x&=2y-20\end{align*}$$

Substitute into (1).

$$\begin{align*}3(2y-20)&=4y\\6y-60&=4y\\2y&=60\\y&=30\\x&=2(30)-20\\x&=40\\x+y&=40+30\\x+y&=70\end{align*}$$

Therefore, 70 votes were cast.

teachingContext.mappingNote: The two voter ratios provide two independent equations in the original male and female counts; simultaneous-word-problems is the most advanced directly assessed skill.

The teacher pixels identify Section F, item 6, as 'A total of 70 votes are cast.' Independent solution gives 40 men and 30 women; the reduced counts 32 and 16 have ratio 2:1, and the original total is 70.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common base share, express the other three shares through it and equate two independently described expressions for Vera's share.

content.prompt: Four friends shared a box of apples. Vera took 4 more than Lynn, and 13 more than Susan. Lynn took twice as many as Diana. Susan took 6 more than Diana. How many apples did each girl take?

answer.short:
Vera: 34 apples; Lynn: 30 apples; Susan: 21 apples; Diana: 15 apples.

Let Diana's share be $x$. Equating the two expressions for Vera's share gives $2x+4=x+19$.
answer.worked:
Let Diana take $x$ apples. Lynn takes $2x$, Susan takes $x+6$, and Vera takes both $2x+4$ and $(x+6)+13$.

$$\begin{align*}2x+4&=(x+6)+13\\2x+4&=x+19\\x+4&=19\\x&=15\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Lynn}&=2(15)=30\\\text{Susan}&=15+6=21\\\text{Vera}&=30+4=34\end{align*}$$

Therefore, Vera took 34 apples, Lynn took 30 apples, Susan took 21 apples and Diana took 15 apples. The remaining relationship also holds: $34-21=13$.

content.prompt: Fatima is thirty years older than her daughter, but is two years younger than her husband. If the sum of their ages is eighty years, then how old is Fatima?

$$\begin{align*}x+(x-30)+(x+2)&=80\\3x-28&=80\\3x&=108\\x&=36\end{align*}$$

Therefore, Fatima is 36 years old.

classification.difficultyReason: Express five candidates’ vote totals using one unknown and combine the linked relationships into a total-votes equation.

content.prompt: In a recent election, 75 votes were cast. Jo received twice as many votes as Tracy. Penny had 9 more than Sue and 6 more than Tracy. Penny had ten times as many votes as Alice. How many votes did each candidate receive?

inlines.text: Jo: 28 votes; Tracy: 14 votes; Penny: 20 votes; Sue: 11 votes; Alice: 2 votes.
Express each share in terms of Penny’s votes and set their sum equal to 75.

answer.worked:
Let $p$ be Penny’s number of votes. Tracy received $p-6$, Jo received $2(p-6)$, Sue received $p-9$, and Alice received $\frac{p}{10}$.

$$\begin{align*}2(p-6)+(p-6)+p+(p-9)+\frac{p}{10}&=75\\5p-27+\frac{p}{10}&=75\\50p-270+p&=750\\51p&=1020\\p&=20\end{align*}$$

Hence Tracy received $20-6=14$ votes, Jo received $2(14)=28$ votes, Sue received $20-9=11$ votes, and Alice received $20\div10=2$ votes. Penny received 20 votes.

Check: $28+14+20+11+2=75$.

teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 12 Example 1 models linked shares with one unknown and a total equation; question 9 assesses the same method with five vote shares.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer possible placings from total points and reconcile the competitors' results across all events.

content.prompt: Adrienne, Binh and Cooper were the only three competitors participating in a series of athletic events. In each event, the winner gets 3 points, second gets 2 points and third gets 1 point. After the events, Adrienne has 8 points, Binh has 11 points and Cooper has 5 points. In how many events did Adrienne come second? Perhaps you can do this without algebra?

answer.short:
Two events.

Binh came second once and Cooper came second once; Adrienne came second in the other two events.
answer.worked:
Each event awards $3+2+1=6$ points. The total is $8+11+5=24$ points, so there were $24\div6=4$ events.

Binh's 11 points are one less than four wins, so Binh won three events and came second once. Cooper's 5 points are one more than four third places, so Cooper came third three times and second once.

Their second places occurred in different events. Adrienne therefore came second in the remaining $4-1-1=2$ events.

teachingContext.methodNote: The inspected introduction establishes equality and equivalent operations. This question explicitly suggests reasoning without algebra; total points and deviations from maximum or minimum scores determine the placings.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Model word problems with equations is the closest catalogue skill for interpreting numerical constraints in context; the authored solution follows the source's explicit invitation to use non-algebraic reasoning.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The supplied student image shows question 10 naming Adrienne, Binh and Cooper with totals 8, 11 and 5. The supplied teacher image's Section F entry 10 states that Adrienne came second in two events, agreeing with the independently derived result.

content.prompt: How tall is the box shown below?

spec.description: Two paired arrangements with aligned ground levels: female on a box and male on the ground at left; male on an identical box and female on the ground at right. Repeated figures have identical heights. Unfilled red and blue outlines distinguish the two people; decorative source fills are omitted.
spec.mathematics: The left head-height difference is 1.4 m and the right head-height difference is 2.1 m. Both double-ended arrows terminate at dashed guides through the respective head tops. Drawing coordinates specify illustrative proportions only, not additional numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied differences are visible; no box height or person height is supplied.

inlines.text: Add the two height differences to obtain twice the box height.

answer.worked:
Let $h$, $f$ and $m$ be the heights in metres of the box, female and male respectively.
$$\begin{align*}
h+f-m&=1.4\\
h+m-f&=2.1
\end{align*}$$
Adding the equations eliminates both people's heights:
$$\begin{align*}
2h&=3.5\\
h&=1.75
\end{align*}$$
The box is $1.75\,\mathrm{m}$ tall.

teachingContext.methodNote: Model the two head-height differences with equations and add them to eliminate opposite coefficients, following the elimination demonstration on teaching PDF page 18.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The assessed step is forming simultaneous equations from a diagram; addition cancels both people's heights and leaves a one-step equation for the box.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows question 11 asking for the box height with differences 1.4 m and 2.1 m. Teacher Section F, item 11, visibly gives 1.75 m, agreeing with the independently derived value (1.4 + 2.1)/2.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer two height-difference equations from paired arrangements and eliminate both people's heights.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the aggregate-distance invariant: every kilometre travelled contributes two kilometres to the sum of tyre usage, regardless of spare changes.

content.prompt:
Dean’s trailer has three tyres. At any given time two of these are used and the third is spare. The three tires have covered different distances: $25\,000$ km, $28\,000$ km, and $31\,000$ km.

Find the total distance that Dean’s trailer has travelled.

answer.short:
$42\,000\text{ km}$

Add the three tyre distances and divide by two, since two tyres are used at any given time.
answer.worked:
Let $d$ be the distance travelled by the trailer, in kilometres. Since two tyres are used at any given time, their combined distance is $2d$.

$$\begin{align*}2d &= 25\,000+28\,000+31\,000\\2d &= 84\,000\\d &= \frac{84\,000}{2}\\d &= 42\,000\end{align*}$$

The trailer has travelled $42\,000\text{ km}$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Define an unknown, express the contextual total as a linear equation, and divide both sides by the same non-zero number.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 12 demonstrates forming an equation from a worded total; page 2 demonstrates division to isolate the unknown. Here the combined tyre distance equals twice the trailer distance.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Source page 27, printed page 48, question 12 gives tyre distances of 25 000 km, 28 000 km and 31 000 km, with two tyres used at any time. The inspected teacher image lists Section F question 12 as 42 000 km. Independently summing the distances gives 84 000 km and dividing by two gives 42 000 km.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that two tyres accumulate distance for each kilometre travelled and model the combined distance.

If three numbers $x$, $y$, and $z$ satisfy
$$\begin{aligned}x+y&=7,\\x+z&=12,\\y+z&=21,\end{aligned}$$
find $x+y+z$.

answer.worked:
Add the three equations.
$$\begin{align*}(x+y)+(x+z)+(y+z)&=7+12+21\\2(x+y+z)&=40\\x+y+z&=20\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
If three numbers $x$, $y$, and $z$ satisfy
$$\begin{aligned}xy&=7,\\xz&=12,\\yz&=21,\end{aligned}$$
find $xyz$.

inlines.text: Multiply the three equations. Both signs are possible because the numbers may all be positive or all negative.

answer.worked:
Multiply the three equations.
$$\begin{align*}(xy)(xz)(yz)&=7\times12\times21\\(xyz)^2&=1764\\xyz&=\pm42\end{align*}$$
Both signs are possible: $(x,y,z)=(2,\frac72,6)$ and $(x,y,z)=(-2,-\frac72,-6)$ satisfy all three equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive equal envelope and money targets, reduce the possible individual shares to integer constraints and coordinate three valid shares that exhaust every envelope type.

content.prompt: There are seven envelopes that each contain $\$7$, ten envelopes that each contain $\$10$, and thirteen envelopes that each contain $\$13$. How can the envelopes be shared between three people so that each person receives the same number of envelopes and the same total amount of money?

answer.short:
One possible distribution, listing the numbers of $\$7$, $\$10$ and $\$13$ envelopes respectively, is $(1,6,3)$, $(2,4,4)$ and $(4,0,6)$.

Each person receives 10 envelopes and $\$106$. Use equal envelope counts and equal money totals to determine the shares.
answer.worked:
There are $7+10+13=30$ envelopes, so each person receives $30\div3=10$ envelopes. The total money is $7(7)+10(10)+13(13)=318$ dollars, so each person receives $318\div3=106$ dollars.

Let $x$ and $y$ be the numbers of $\$7$ and $\$10$ envelopes received by one person. Their number of $\$13$ envelopes is $10-x-y$.

$$\begin{align*}7x+10y+13(10-x-y)&=106\\7x+10y+130-13x-13y&=106\\-6x-3y&=-24\\2x+y&=8\\y&=8-2x\end{align*}$$

Choosing $x=1,2,4$ gives shares $(x,y,10-x-y)$ of $(1,6,3)$, $(2,4,4)$ and $(4,0,6)$.

These use $1+2+4=7$ envelopes containing $\$7$, $6+4+0=10$ containing $\$10$, and $3+4+6=13$ containing $\$13$. Each share has 10 envelopes, and the money totals are $7+60+39=106$, $14+40+52=106$ and $28+78=106$ dollars.

teachingContext.methodNote: Define unknown quantities, express related quantities in terms of them, form an equation from the total, expand and simplify, and apply equivalent operations to both sides.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 12 Example 1 models shared money using related algebraic amounts. This question extends that method to equal envelope counts and equal monetary shares, requiring integer choices.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Source page 27 question 14 gives seven $7, ten $10 and thirteen $13 envelopes shared equally among three people. Teacher page 8 Section F question 14 states 10 envelopes and $106 per person, derives 2x+y=8, and explicitly gives distributions (1,6,3), (2,4,4) and (4,0,6). Independent count and money checks agree with those printed shares.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires modelling equal shares and finding compatible non-negative integer envelope counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the bounded integer average of seven students to express the total, then apply divisibility by ten to identify the unique possible overall average.

content.prompt: Ten students sit a test consisting of twenty questions. Two students get eight questions correct and one student gets nine questions correct. The remaining seven students all get at least ten questions correct and the average number of questions answered correctly by these seven students is an integer. If the average number of questions answered correctly by all ten students is also an integer, then find that integer.

inlines.text: 13 questions.
The seven students must average 15 for the overall average to be an integer.

answer.worked:
Let $k$ be the integer average for the remaining seven students. Since each answers between 10 and 20 questions correctly, $10\le k\le20$. Their total score is $7k$.

The overall average is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{8+8+9+7k}{10}&=\frac{25+7k}{10}.\end{align*}$$
For this to be an integer, $25+7k$ must be divisible by 10. Hence $7k$ must end in 5, so $k$ must end in 5. The only such integer between 10 and 20 is $k=15$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{25+7(15)}{10}&=\frac{130}{10}\\\frac{25+7(15)}{10}&=13.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, the average for all ten students is 13 questions.

teachingContext.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral for an unknown quantity, express the related totals algebraically, and use exact arithmetic and equivalent expressions. The integer constraint additionally requires elementary divisibility reasoning.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Question 15 is a worded model involving an unknown integer average; model-word-problems-equations is the closest catalogue skill. Teaching page 12 demonstrates forming algebraic totals from a worded context.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Source page 27 question 15 specifies two scores of 8, one of 9, and seven integer-average scores bounded by 10 and 20. Teacher page 8 Section F answer 15 uses (25+7k)/10, derives k=15, and gives the overall average as 13. Independent calculation agrees: (25+105)/10=13.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model the total score using an integer average and combine score bounds with divisibility to determine a unique answer.

content.prompt: Today, in a ten-member committee, an old member was replaced by a young member. The average age is now the same as it was four years ago. Find the difference in ages between the old member and the young member.

answer.short:
40 years.

The replacement reduces the total age by $10\times4=40$ years.
answer.worked:
Let $s$ be the total age of the ten members before the replacement, and $d$ the difference between the old member’s and young member’s ages. Four years ago, the total age was $s-40$; after the replacement, it is $s-d$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{s-d}{10}&=\frac{s-40}{10}\\s-d&=s-40\\-d&=-40\\d&=40\end{align*}$$

The old member is 40 years older than the young member.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires relating a replacement’s effect on total age to a four-year change in the average of ten members.

teachingContext.methodNote: Define unknown quantities, express contextual totals algebraically, equate the averages, and perform equivalent operations on both sides.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is forming an equation from the committee’s age information; solving the resulting equation uses elementary inverse operations.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Source question 16 describes replacing a member of a ten-member committee while restoring the average age from four years earlier. Teacher Section F question 16 models the same totals as (x-d)/10=(x-40)/10 and gives d=40, agreeing with the independently derived difference of 40 years.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires relating a replacement’s effect on total age to a four-year change in the average of ten members.

classification.difficultyReason: Untangle the nested past-and-present age comparison, determine the common elapsed time and express the wife's age then before combining with the current total.

content.prompt: Mr Smith’s current age is exactly twice his wife’s age when he was six years older than she is now. Their combined current age is 53. How old are they?

answer.short:
Mr Smith is 32 years old and Mrs Smith is 21 years old.

Use the same elapsed time for both ages to form simultaneous equations.
answer.worked:
Let $S$ and $W$ be Mr and Mrs Smith’s current ages in years. When Mr Smith was $W+6$ years old, the elapsed time was $S-(W+6)$ years, so his wife’s age then was $W-[S-(W+6)]$.

$$\begin{align*}S+W&=53\\S&=2\bigl(W-[S-(W+6)]\bigr)\\S&=4W-2S+12\\3S&=4W+12\end{align*}$$

Substitute $S=53-W$:

$$\begin{align*}3(53-W)&=4W+12\\159-3W&=4W+12\\147&=7W\\W&=21\\S&=53-21\\S&=32\end{align*}$$

Mr Smith is 32 years old and Mrs Smith is 21 years old. Five years ago their ages were 27 and 16: $27=21+6$ and $32=2(16)$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Define unknowns, translate the conditions into simultaneous equations, substitute an expression for one unknown, and solve using equivalent equations.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 19 models worded conditions with two unknowns; page 17 demonstrates substitution. Here the past-age condition supplies one equation and the combined current age supplies the other.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows the current/past-age condition and combined age 53. Teacher Section F question 17 defines S and W, uses S=2(W-(S-(W+6))) with S+W=53, and gives Mr Smith 32 and Mrs Smith 21. Independent substitution produces the same ages and satisfies both conditions.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing present and past ages and modelling the elapsed time before solving simultaneous equations.

entries.description:
2A Introduction
Let a, b and c be real numbers. A linear equation is any equation that can be put in the form ax + b = c, where x is some unknown number. For example,
2x + 3 = 4
is a typical linear equation. A solution of a linear equation is any value of x that makes the equation true.

entries.description:
Linear equations can contain more than one unknown. A linear equation in the unknowns x and y is any equation of the form ax + by = c where a, b, and c are real numbers. A system of linear equations is a collection of two or more linear equations involving the same set of unknowns. These are also referred to as simultaneous equations. For example,
3x + 2y = 5
2x − 3y = 12
is a system of equations whose unknowns are x and y. The aim is to find a solution to all the equations in the system. A solution to a linear system consists of values of the unknowns for which the equations are simultaneously satisfied.

entries.description:
By equating equations (1) and (2) we obtain
3x − 1 = 2x + 1    (1) = (2)
x − 1 = 1    (−2x)
x = 2    (+1)
Having found the value of x, we find y by substituting x = 2 into equation (2). This gives
y = 2x + 1 = 2(2) + 1 = 5.
We could also have substituted x = 2 into equation (2) and obtained the same value of y:
y = 3x − 1 = 3(2) − 1 = 5.
In general, we substitute into the equation that is most easily solved.
Therefore, the solution of our system of equations is (x, y) = (2, 5).

entries.description:
We can also solve simultaneous equations by adding or subtracting the equations in a way that eliminates one of the unknowns from the resulting equation. This is called the elimination method. When solving simultaneous linear equations by this method the choice to add or subtract depends on the coefficients of the variable to be eliminated:
• Add the equations if the coefficients of the chosen variable have opposite signs, so they cancel out.
• Subtract the equations if the coefficients of the chosen variable have the same signs, so they cancel out.
Again, this is best understood via an example.

entries.description:
Consider the system,
2x + 3y = 12 (1)
3x + 2y = 13 (2)
Notice that adding or subtracting these two equations will not eliminate either x or y, as there is no matching pair of coefficients. When this happens, we must first scale one or both equations to prepare for the elimination step. Multiplying (1) by 3 and (2) by 2 give an equivalent system of equations:
(1) × 3    6x + 9y = 36 (3)
(2) × 2    6x + 4y = 26 (4)
Subtracting (4) from (3) would then eliminate the x unknown.

entries.description: A coffee maker sells a total of 50 coffees for a total of $180. Each regular coffee costs $3 and each large coffee costs $4.50. How many regular and how many large coffees are sold?
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone worked example; reference evidence only under the practice-only scope.

entries.description:
Let R and L be the number of regular and large coffees that are sold, respectively. From the information given, we form two equations:
R + L = 50 (1)
3R + 4.5L = 180 (2)
These two equations are recast as follows:
R + L = 50
⇒ R = 50 − L (3)
3R + 4.5L = 180
⇒ 6R + 9L = 360 (4)
Substituting the the expression for R in (3) into equation (4) gives
6(50 − L) + 9L = 360
300 − 6L + 9L = 360
300 + 3L = 360
3L = 60
L = 20
Substituting L = 20 into equation (1) gives R = 30. Therefore, 20 large coffees and 30 regular coffees were sold.

entries.description:
The coefficient of x is the same in each equation. Therefore, this unknown can be eliminated as follows.
 x + y + 2z = 5 (1)
 x + 2y + 3z = 3 (2)
 x + 2y + z = 1 (3)
 (2) − (1): y + z = −2 (4)
 (3) − (1): y − z = −4 (5)
 (4) + (5): 2y = −6
 y = −3
 z = 1 (sub. y = −3 in (4))
 x = 6 (sub. y = −3 and z = 1 in (1))

entries.description:
We let the three unknowns be x, y and z. Then,
 x + y = 7 (1)
 x + z = 3 (2)
 y + z = 12 (3)
 2x + 2y + 2z = 22 (1) + (2) + (3)
 x + y + z = 11 (4)
We can substitute equation (1) into (4) to find z:
 (x + y) + z = 11
 7 + z = 11
 z = 4
